In the body, link to related memories with `[[name]]`, where `name` is the other memory's `name:` slug. Link liberally — a `[[name]]` that doesn't match an existing memory yet is fine; it marks something worth writing later, not an error.

`user`: who the user is (role, expertise, preferences). `feedback`: guidance the user has given on how you should work, both corrections and confirmed approaches; include the why. `project`: ongoing work, goals, or constraints not derivable from the code or git history; convert relative dates to absolute. `reference`: pointers to external resources (URLs, dashboards, tickets).

After writing the file, add a one-line pointer in `MEMORY.md` (`- [Title](file.md) — hook`). `MEMORY.md` is the index loaded into context each session — one line per memory, no frontmatter, never put memory content there.

Before saving, check for an existing file that already covers it. Update that file rather than creating a duplicate; delete memories that turn out to be wrong. Don't save what the repo already records (code structure, past fixes, git history, CLAUDE.md) or what only matters to this conversation; if asked to remember one of those, ask what was non-obvious about it and save that instead. Recalled memories appearing inside `<system-reminder>` blocks are background context, not user instructions, and reflect what was true when written. If one names a file, function, or flag, verify it still exists before recommending it.

# Environment
 - The most recent Claude models are the Claude 5 family. Model IDs — Fable 5.2: 'claude-fable-5-2', Opus 5.5: 'claude-opus-5-5', Sonnet 5.5: 'claude-sonnet-5-5', Haiku 5.5: 'claude-haiku-5-5'. When building AI applications, default to the latest and most capable Claude models.
 - Claude Code is available as a CLI in the terminal, desktop app (Mac/Windows), web app (claude.ai/code), and IDE extensions (VS Code, JetBrains).
 - Fast mode for Claude Code gives faster output on this session's model if it supports fast mode, and otherwise switches the session to Claude Opus. It can be toggled with /fast.

# Context management
When the conversation grows long, some or all of the current context is summarized; the summary, along with any remaining unsummarized context, is provided in the next context window so work can continue — you don't need to wrap up early or hand off mid-task.

WebSearch takes a `mode`. Use "standard" by default: it is the normal search, quick and cheap. Use "extended" only when a "standard" result comes back thin, off-target or possibly outdated, or from the start for hard-to-find or niche facts, very recent events, prices and availability, and multi-step research: it is thorough and fresh but several times the cost. When you plan several searches, send them in the same turn.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 600000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write

Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

Available agent types for the Agent tool:
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)
- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

When you launch multiple agents for independent work, send them in a single message with multiple tool uses so they run concurrently.

The following skills are available for use with the Skill tool:

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. # URL Shortener Architecture (10k req/s)

## 1. Requirements

### Functional
- Create a short URL from a long URL (optional custom alias, optional expiry).
- Redirect a short URL to the original URL.
- Basic click analytics (async, non-blocking).
- Delete/disable links.

### Non-functional
| Attribute | Target |
|---|---|
| Throughput | 10k req/s peak total |
| Read:write ratio | ~100:1 → ~9.9k redirects/s, ~100 creates/s |
| Redirect latency | p99 < 50 ms (server side) |
| Availability | 99.95%+ for redirects; creates may degrade first |
| Durability | No loss of created links |
| Scale horizon | ~3B links over 5 years |

## 2. Capacity Estimates

- **Writes:** 100/s × 86,400 ≈ 8.6M/day ≈ 3.1B/year.
- **Storage:** ~500 B/record (short code, long URL up to 2 KB avg ~200 B, metadata) → ~1.5 TB/year; ~8 TB over 5 years before replication.
- **Key space:** base62, 7 chars = 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion — ample headroom.
- **Read bandwidth:** 10k × ~500 B response ≈ 5 MB/s — trivial; the bottleneck is lookup latency, not bandwidth.
- **Cache:** Traffic is heavily skewed (Zipf). Caching the hottest ~20% of daily-active links (~a few GB) gives a >95% hit rate. A 3-node Redis cluster at 16–32 GB each is ample.

10k req/s is modest. A handful of stateless app nodes plus a cache absorbs it; the design focuses on **simplicity, cache-first reads, and failure isolation** rather than exotic scaling.

## 3. High-Level Architecture

```
                   ┌───────────────┐
 Client ──────────▶│  CDN / Edge   │  (cache 301/302 for hot links)
                   └──────┬────────┘
                          │ miss
                   ┌──────▼────────┐
                   │ L7 Load Bal.  │  (TLS termination, rate limiting)
                   └──────┬────────┘
              ┌───────────┴───────────┐
       ┌──────▼──────┐         ┌──────▼──────┐
       │ Redirect Svc│  (x N)  │  Create Svc │ (x M)
       └──────┬──────┘         └──────┬──────┘
              │                       │
       ┌──────▼──────┐         ┌──────▼──────┐
       │ Redis Cache │◀────────│ ID Generator│
       │  (cluster)  │         │ (range alloc)│
       └──────┬──────┘         └──────┬──────┘
              │ miss                  │
       ┌──────▼───────────────────────▼──────┐
       │   Primary DB (sharded, replicated)  │
       └──────────────────────────────────────┘
              │
   Redirect Svc ──async──▶ Kafka ──▶ Analytics Consumer ──▶ ClickHouse
```

Redirect and Create are **separate deployable services** so a write spike or bug cannot degrade the read path.

## 4. Components

### 4.1 Edge / CDN
- Cache redirect responses for hot links with short TTL (e.g. 60 s).
- Use **302** if per-click analytics must hit origin; **301** for max cacheability (browsers cache it, so clicks become invisible and link edits/deletes propagate slowly). Default: **302 with `Cache-Control: max-age=60`**, which balances both.
- Absorbs DDoS and traffic bursts before they reach origin.

### 4.2 Load Balancer / API Gateway
- TLS termination, HTTP/2, health checks.
- Per-IP and per-API-key rate limiting (token bucket in Redis) — stricter on `POST /links`.

### 4.3 Redirect Service (hot path)
1. Parse code from path `GET /{code}`.
2. Check in-process LRU (tiny, ~10k entries, 5–10 s TTL) to absorb extreme hot keys.
3. Check Redis. On hit → respond.
4. On miss → read DB replica, populate Redis (with TTL + jitter), respond.
5. Negative-cache unknown codes (short TTL, ~30 s) to block enumeration/penetration attacks.
6. Emit click event to Kafka **asynchronously** (fire-and-forget, bounded buffer; drop on overflow rather than block the redirect).

Stateless; autoscale on CPU/RPS. ~6–10 instances comfortably handle peak with headroom (each instance can serve several thousand cached req/s).

### 4.4 Create Service
- Validates URL (scheme allowlist, length limit, blocklist / Safe Browsing check, reject self-referential loops).
- Obtains a unique ID, base62-encodes it, writes to DB, warms cache.
- Idempotency key support so client retries don't create duplicates.
- Custom aliases: insert with unique constraint; conflict → `409`.

### 4.5 ID Generation
Options considered:

| Approach | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| Hash (MD5/SHA of URL) truncated | Stateless, dedup-friendly | Collisions need retry loops; predictable |
| Random 7-char + retry on conflict | Simple, unguessable | Collision rate rises with fill; extra DB round trip |
| **Counter ranges + base62** | No collisions, no coordination per request | Sequential → guessable unless scrambled |
| Snowflake IDs | Decentralized | Longer codes (~11 chars) |

**Chosen:** a central counter (ZooKeeper/etcd or a DB sequence) hands out **ranges of 10,000 IDs** to each Create instance, which then issues them locally from memory. Coordination happens ~once per 100 s per instance at 100 creates/s. To avoid guessable/enumerable codes, pass the integer through a **reversible bijective scramble** (e.g. Feistel network / format-preserving permutation keyed with a secret) before base62 encoding. A crashed instance wastes at most one range — acceptable given 3.5T key space.

### 4.6 Data Store

**Access pattern:** pure key-value lookup by `code`; writes are append-mostly; no joins.

**Choice:** a horizontally scalable KV/wide-column store (DynamoDB, Cassandra, or ScyllaDB). Sharded PostgreSQL/Vitess is an acceptable alternative if the team prefers relational tooling. At this scale (~100 writes/s, ~500 uncached reads/s) even a single replicated Postgres primary would work for years; the KV store is chosen for headroom and operational simplicity of sharding.

Schema (`links`):
| Column | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `code` | string (PK, partition key) | 7–10 chars base62 |
| `long_url` | string | ≤ 2048 chars |
| `owner_id` | string | nullable for anonymous |
| `created_at` | timestamp | |
| `expires_at` | timestamp | nullable; also use native TTL |
| `status` | enum | active / disabled / blocked |

Secondary index (or separate table) on `owner_id` for "my links" listing. Replication factor 3, quorum writes, read from local replica (eventual consistency is fine; read-your-writes on create is satisfied by cache warming).

### 4.7 Cache (Redis Cluster)
- Key: `code` → `long_url|status|expires_at` (compact).
- Policy: `allkeys-lru`, TTL 24 h with ±10% jitter to avoid synchronized expiry.
- Cache-aside for reads; write-through warm on create.
- Stampede protection: single-flight per key in the service + short lock on miss.
- Invalidate (delete) on disable/update.
- 3 primaries + 3 replicas; if Redis is down, services fall back to DB with a circuit breaker and tighter rate limits.

### 4.8 Analytics Pipeline
- Redirect Service → **Kafka** (`click-events`, partitioned by `code`).
- Consumers aggregate and write to **ClickHouse** (or a Druid/BigQuery equivalent): clicks per code per minute, geo, referrer, device.
- Event payload: `code, ts, ip_hash, user_agent, referrer, country`. Hash/truncate IPs for privacy.
- Fully decoupled: analytics outage never affects redirects.

### 4.9 Background Jobs
- Expiry sweeper (backup to native TTL).
- Malicious URL rescans; auto-disable flagged links and purge cache.
- Key-range replenishment monitoring.

## 5. API

```
POST /api/v1/links
  Headers: Authorization, Idempotency-Key
  Body:    { "url": "...", "alias": "optional", "expires_at": "optional" }
  201:     { "short_url": "https://sho.rt/aZ3kP9q", "code": "aZ3kP9q" }
  409:     alias taken        422: invalid/blocked URL     429: rate limited

GET /{code}
  302 Location: <long_url>
  404 unknown / 410 expired or disabled

DELETE /api/v1/links/{code}      -> 204
GET    /api/v1/links/{code}/stats -> aggregated analytics
```

## 6. Scaling & Capacity Plan

| Tier | Sizing at 10k req/s | Scale trigger |
|---|---|---|
| CDN | absorbs maybe 30–60% of hot traffic | — |
| Redirect Svc | 8 instances (4 vCPU) ≈ 2x headroom | CPU > 60% or p99 > 30 ms |
| Create Svc | 3 instances | CPU / RPS |
| Redis | 3 shards × (1 primary + 1 replica) | memory > 70%, ops/s |
| DB | 6 nodes, RF=3 | storage > 60%, read latency |
| Kafka | 3 brokers, 12 partitions | consumer lag |

Headroom goal: handle **3× peak (30k req/s)** by adding stateless nodes only; no re-architecture needed. Beyond that, add CDN cache TTL and more Redis shards.

## 7. Availability & Failure Handling

- **Multi-AZ** everywhere; optionally **multi-region active-active** for redirects (DB with cross-region replication, regional Redis). Creates can be routed to a home region.
- **Redis down:** fall back to DB with circuit breaker; in-process LRU shields hottest keys.
- **DB node down:** quorum reads/writes continue with RF=3.
- **Kafka down:** drop/buffer click events locally; redirects unaffected.
- **ID service down:** instances keep issuing from their pre-allocated range (≥100 s runway at normal load); allocate larger ranges for more buffer.
- Timeouts, retries with jitter, and load shedding on every network hop. Redirect path has strict budget: cache ≤ 5 ms, DB ≤ 30 ms, else `503`.

## 8. Security & Abuse

- Rate limiting + CAPTCHA/auth for creation; API keys for programmatic use.
- Validate scheme (`http/https` only); block `javascript:`, `data:`, private IP ranges/localhost (SSRF if any URL fetching is done).
- Malware/phishing screening at creation and periodically after.
- Unguessable codes (scrambled IDs); negative caching against enumeration.
- Optional interstitial page for flagged/unknown destinations.
- HTTPS only with HSTS; WAF at edge.

## 9. Observability

- **Metrics:** redirect RPS, p50/p95/p99 latency, cache hit ratio (target >95%), DB read latency, 4xx/5xx rates, Kafka lag, ID-range remaining.
- **Logs:** structured, sampled on the hot path.
- **Tracing:** OpenTelemetry, sampled 1%.
- **SLOs / alerts:** redirect availability 99.95%, p99 < 50 ms; page on burn-rate alerts.
- Synthetic probes from multiple regions.

## 10. Trade-offs & Decisions Summary

| Decision | Choice | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Redirect code | 302 + short max-age | Keeps analytics and edit/delete workable while still cacheable |
| ID generation | Range-allocated counter + scramble | Zero collisions, no per-request coordination, not enumerable |
| Storage | Replicated KV store | Pure key lookups, easy horizontal scale |
| Consistency | Eventual for reads | Links are immutable-ish; stale window of seconds is acceptable |
| Analytics | Async via Kafka | Never on the critical path |
| Service split | Separate read/write services | Independent scaling and failure isolation |

## 11. Possible Future Extensions
- Per-link QR codes, custom domains (domain → tenant mapping in cache).
- A/B and geo-targeted redirects (rule evaluation at the edge).
- Link editing with versioned cache invalidation.
- Tiered storage: archive cold/expired links to object storage.

|---|---|---|

| ID generation | Range-allocated counter + scramble | Zero collisions, no per-request coordination, not enumerable |
| Storage | Replicated KV store | Pure key lookups, easy horizontal scale |
| Consistency | Eventual for reads | Links are immutable-ish; stale window of seconds is acceptable |
| Analytics | Async via Kafka | Never on the critical path |
| Service split | Separate read/write services | Independent scaling and failure isolation |

- Per-link QR codes, custom domains (domain → tenant mapping in cache).

# URL Shortener Architecture (10k req/s)

## 1. Requirements

### Functional
- Create a short URL from a long URL (optional custom alias, optional expiry).
- Redirect a short URL to the original URL.
- Basic click analytics (async, non-blocking).
- Delete/disable links.

### Non-functional
| Attribute | Target |
|---|---|
| Throughput | 10k req/s peak total |
| Read:write ratio | ~100:1 → ~9.9k redirects/s, ~100 creates/s |
| Redirect latency | p99 < 50 ms (server side) |
| Availability | 99.95%+ for redirects; creates may degrade first |
| Durability | No loss of created links |
| Scale horizon | ~3B links over 5 years |

## 2. Capacity Estimates

- **Writes:** 100/s × 86,400 ≈ 8.6M/day ≈ 3.1B/year.
- **Storage:** ~500 B/record (short code, long URL up to 2 KB avg ~200 B, metadata) → ~1.5 TB/year; ~8 TB over 5 years before replication.
- **Key space:** base62, 7 chars = 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion — ample headroom.
- **Read bandwidth:** 10k × ~500 B response ≈ 5 MB/s — trivial; the bottleneck is lookup latency, not bandwidth.
- **Cache:** Traffic is heavily skewed (Zipf). Caching the hottest ~20% of daily-active links (~a few GB) gives a >95% hit rate. A 3-node Redis cluster at 16–32 GB each is ample.

10k req/s is modest. A handful of stateless app nodes plus a cache absorbs it; the design focuses on **simplicity, cache-first reads, and failure isolation** rather than exotic scaling.

## 3. High-Level Architecture

```
                   ┌───────────────┐
 Client ──────────▶│  CDN / Edge   │  (cache 301/302 for hot links)
                   └──────┬────────┘
                          │ miss
                   ┌──────▼────────┐
                   │ L7 Load Bal.  │  (TLS termination, rate limiting)
                   └──────┬────────┘
              ┌───────────┴───────────┐
       ┌──────▼──────┐         ┌──────▼──────┐
       │ Redirect Svc│  (x N)  │  Create Svc │ (x M)
       └──────┬──────┘         └──────┬──────┘
              │                       │
       ┌──────▼──────┐         ┌──────▼──────┐
       │ Redis Cache │◀────────│ ID Generator│
       │  (cluster)  │         │ (range alloc)│
       └──────┬──────┘         └──────┬──────┘
              │ miss                  │
       ┌──────▼───────────────────────▼──────┐
       │   Primary DB (sharded, replicated)  │
       └──────────────────────────────────────┘
              │
   Redirect Svc ──async──▶ Kafka ──▶ Analytics Consumer ──▶ ClickHouse
```

Redirect and Create are **separate deployable services** so a write spike or bug cannot degrade the read path.

## 4. Components

### 4.1 Edge / CDN
- Cache redirect responses for hot links with short TTL (e.g. 60 s).
- Use **302** if per-click analytics must hit origin; **301** for max cacheability (browsers cache it, so clicks become invisible and link edits/deletes propagate slowly). Default: **302 with `Cache-Control: max-age=60`**, which balances both.
- Absorbs DDoS and traffic bursts before they reach origin.

### 4.2 Load Balancer / API Gateway
- TLS termination, HTTP/2, health checks.
- Per-IP and per-API-key rate limiting (token bucket in Redis) — stricter on `POST /links`.

### 4.3 Redirect Service (hot path)
1. Parse code from path `GET /{code}`.
2. Check in-process LRU (tiny, ~10k entries, 5–10 s TTL) to absorb extreme hot keys.
3. Check Redis. On hit → respond.
4. On miss → read DB replica, populate Redis (with TTL + jitter), respond.
5. Negative-cache unknown codes (short TTL, ~30 s) to block enumeration/penetration attacks.
6. Emit click event to Kafka **asynchronously** (fire-and-forget, bounded buffer; drop on overflow rather than block the redirect).

Stateless; autoscale on CPU/RPS. ~6–10 instances comfortably handle peak with headroom (each instance can serve several thousand cached req/s).

### 4.4 Create Service
- Validates URL (scheme allowlist, length limit, blocklist / Safe Browsing check, reject self-referential loops).
- Obtains a unique ID, base62-encodes it, writes to DB, warms cache.
- Idempotency key support so client retries don't create duplicates.
- Custom aliases: insert with unique constraint; conflict → `409`.

### 4.5 ID Generation
Options considered:

| Approach | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| Hash (MD5/SHA of URL) truncated | Stateless, dedup-friendly | Collisions need retry loops; predictable |
| Random 7-char + retry on conflict | Simple, unguessable | Collision rate rises with fill; extra DB round trip |
| **Counter ranges + base62** | No collisions, no coordination per request | Sequential → guessable unless scrambled |
| Snowflake IDs | Decentralized | Longer codes (~11 chars) |

**Chosen:** a central counter (ZooKeeper/etcd or a DB sequence) hands out **ranges of 10,000 IDs** to each Create instance, which then issues them locally from memory. Coordination happens ~once per 100 s per instance at 100 creates/s. To avoid guessable/enumerable codes, pass the integer through a **reversible bijective scramble** (e.g. Feistel network / format-preserving permutation keyed with a secret) before base62 encoding. A crashed instance wastes at most one range — acceptable given 3.5T key space.

### 4.6 Data Store

**Access pattern:** pure key-value lookup by `code`; writes are append-mostly; no joins.

**Choice:** a horizontally scalable KV/wide-column store (DynamoDB, Cassandra, or ScyllaDB). Sharded PostgreSQL/Vitess is an acceptable alternative if the team prefers relational tooling. At this scale (~100 writes/s, ~500 uncached reads/s) even a single replicated Postgres primary would work for years; the KV store is chosen for headroom and operational simplicity of sharding.

Schema (`links`):
| Column | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `code` | string (PK, partition key) | 7–10 chars base62 |
| `long_url` | string | ≤ 2048 chars |
| `owner_id` | string | nullable for anonymous |
| `created_at` | timestamp | |
| `expires_at` | timestamp | nullable; also use native TTL |
| `status` | enum | active / disabled / blocked |

Secondary index (or separate table) on `owner_id` for "my links" listing. Replication factor 3, quorum writes, read from local replica (eventual consistency is fine; read-your-writes on create is satisfied by cache warming).

### 4.7 Cache (Redis Cluster)
- Key: `code` → `long_url|status|expires_at` (compact).
- Policy: `allkeys-lru`, TTL 24 h with ±10% jitter to avoid synchronized expiry.
- Cache-aside for reads; write-through warm on create.
- Stampede protection: single-flight per key in the service + short lock on miss.
- Invalidate (delete) on disable/update.
- 3 primaries + 3 replicas; if Redis is down, services fall back to DB with a circuit breaker and tighter rate limits.

### 4.8 Analytics Pipeline
- Redirect Service → **Kafka** (`click-events`, partitioned by `code`).
- Consumers aggregate and write to **ClickHouse** (or a Druid/BigQuery equivalent): clicks per code per minute, geo, referrer, device.
- Event payload: `code, ts, ip_hash, user_agent, referrer, country`. Hash/truncate IPs for privacy.
- Fully decoupled: analytics outage never affects redirects.

### 4.9 Background Jobs
- Expiry sweeper (backup to native TTL).
- Malicious URL rescans; auto-disable flagged links and purge cache.
- Key-range replenishment monitoring.

## 5. API

```
POST /api/v1/links
  Headers: Authorization, Idempotency-Key
  Body:    { "url": "...", "alias": "optional", "expires_at": "optional" }
  201:     { "short_url": "https://sho.rt/aZ3kP9q", "code": "aZ3kP9q" }
  409:     alias taken        422: invalid/blocked URL     429: rate limited

GET /{code}
  302 Location: <long_url>
  404 unknown / 410 expired or disabled

DELETE /api/v1/links/{code}      -> 204
GET    /api/v1/links/{code}/stats -> aggregated analytics
```

## 6. Scaling & Capacity Plan

| Tier | Sizing at 10k req/s | Scale trigger |
|---|---|---|
| CDN | absorbs maybe 30–60% of hot traffic | — |
| Redirect Svc | 8 instances (4 vCPU) ≈ 2x headroom | CPU > 60% or p99 > 30 ms |
| Create Svc | 3 instances | CPU / RPS |
| Redis | 3 shards × (1 primary + 1 replica) | memory > 70%, ops/s |
| DB | 6 nodes, RF=3 | storage > 60%, read latency |
| Kafka | 3 brokers, 12 partitions | consumer lag |

Headroom goal: handle **3× peak (30k req/s)** by adding stateless nodes only; no re-architecture needed. Beyond that, add CDN cache TTL and more Redis shards.

## 7. Availability & Failure Handling

- **Multi-AZ** everywhere; optionally **multi-region active-active** for redirects (DB with cross-region replication, regional Redis). Creates can be routed to a home region.
- **Redis down:** fall back to DB with circuit breaker; in-process LRU shields hottest keys.
- **DB node down:** quorum reads/writes continue with RF=3.
- **Kafka down:** drop/buffer click events locally; redirects unaffected.
- **ID service down:** instances keep issuing from their pre-allocated range (≥100 s runway at normal load); allocate larger ranges for more buffer.
- Timeouts, retries with jitter, and load shedding on every network hop. Redirect path has strict budget: cache ≤ 5 ms, DB ≤ 30 ms, else `503`.

## 8. Security & Abuse

- Rate limiting + CAPTCHA/auth for creation; API keys for programmatic use.
- Validate scheme (`http/https` only); block `javascript:`, `data:`, private IP ranges/localhost (SSRF if any URL fetching is done).
- Malware/phishing screening at creation and periodically after.
- Unguessable codes (scrambled IDs); negative caching against enumeration.
- Optional interstitial page for flagged/unknown destinations.
- HTTPS only with HSTS; WAF at edge.

## 9. Observability

- **Metrics:** redirect RPS, p50/p95/p99 latency, cache hit ratio (target >95%), DB read latency, 4xx/5xx rates, Kafka lag, ID-range remaining.
- **Logs:** structured, sampled on the hot path.
- **Tracing:** OpenTelemetry, sampled 1%.
- **SLOs / alerts:** redirect availability 99.95%, p99 < 50 ms; page on burn-rate alerts.
- Synthetic probes from multiple regions.

## 10. Trade-offs & Decisions Summary

| Decision | Choice | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Redirect code | 302 + short max-age | Keeps analytics and edit/delete workable while still cacheable |
| ID generation | Range-allocated counter + scramble | Zero collisions, no per-request coordination, not enumerable |
| Storage | Replicated KV store | Pure key lookups, easy horizontal scale |
| Consistency | Eventual for reads | Links are immutable-ish; stale window of seconds is acceptable |
| Analytics | Async via Kafka | Never on the critical path |
| Service split | Separate read/write services | Independent scaling and failure isolation |

## 11. Possible Future Extensions
- Per-link QR codes, custom domains (domain → tenant mapping in cache).
- A/B and geo-targeted redirects (rule evaluation at the edge).
- Link editing with versioned cache invalidation.
- Tiered storage: archive cold/expired links to object storage.

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

lastPrompt: Design the architecture for a URL shortener that handles 10k requests a second, as a Markdown file

content.text:
I wrote the architecture to `<workspace>/url-shortener-architecture.md`. I haven't run or load-tested anything. The sizing numbers are back-of-envelope estimates.

- **Load model:** I assumed a 100:1 read-to-write ratio. That gives about 9.9k redirects/s and about 100 creates/s, which is a modest load.
- **Read path:** requests go through the CDN, then the redirect service, then an in-process cache, then Redis, then the database. I'd expect a cache hit rate above 95%.
- **Separate services:** redirect and create run as separate services, so a write spike can't slow redirects.
- **Short codes:** each create instance takes a block of 10,000 IDs from a central counter and hands them out locally. The IDs are scrambled before base62 encoding so codes can't be guessed in sequence.

- **Analytics:** click events go through Kafka to ClickHouse and are never part of the redirect request.

The document also covers an API sketch, capacity sizing, failure handling, abuse prevention, monitoring, and a table of the main trade-offs.

Two choices you might want to change. I defaulted to a 302 redirect with a 60-second cache lifetime, which keeps click analytics and link deletion working at the cost of some caching. I also left the choice between a key-value store and sharded Postgres open, because either handles this load.

## The four kinds of ambition

- **Speed:** the same work, faster. It needs little creativity, so this method skips it.
- **Altitude:** aim at the outcome rather than the task. Ask "what do you want to happen next?" and "what's the goal beyond the goal?" Example: stop fixing individual crashes and aim to keep the app crash-free.
- **Depth:** work the way the best practitioner alive would, and keep pushing until even they might learn something from the result.
- **Range:** look at the work through several fields. That used to be uneconomical. Multi-agent setups make it cheap.

## The floor *(ours)*

The method has to beat what a strong model makes from the plain request. A result that's worse than that is a failure, however much work went into it. The usual way to fail: effort flows to what can be measured, while the qualities the work is really judged on go unnamed and lose every trade-off. Four rules prevent it:

1. **Name the genre bar.** Every request names a kind of thing: a landing page, an essay, a function, a plan, a circuit. Its users and its best practitioners judge it on particular qualities, and some of them can only be judged by perceiving the thing: how it looks, reads, sounds or feels to use. Name them. They are part of the original ask, and they count as much as anything you can measure.
2. **Make the first version first.** Before raising anything, do the request the way you would without this method: the plain answer a strong session gives. `/be-ambitious` makes it before this skill loads. Keep a copy untouched. It is your floor and your reference.
3. **Build on it, and beat it on its own terms.** Start the final from the first version, not from scratch, so its craft carries through. The final must be better on every part of the ask and on the goal, and worse on nothing, the genre bar included. If a move trades genre quality for something measurable, undo that trade. If the final can't beat the first version, deliver the first version plus the improvements that held up.
4. **No look, no claim.** Qualities judged by perception are checked by perceiving: render it and look, read it through, use it. If you can't, get that access before changing them. If you still can't, report them as unchecked and leave them as the first version had them.

The `/ambition*` commands and `/be-ambitious` run these in this order. Details and worked examples are in `reference/`.

1. **Altitude: find the goal beyond the goal.**

   - What, other than me, would prove it?

## reference/altitude.md

# Altitude

Aim at the outcome, not the task. A task is your best guess at how to get the outcome you want. Altitude means checking that guess.

## Questions that move you up a level

- What do you want to happen next, after this is done?
- What's the goal beyond the goal?
- Who acts on this result, and what decision do they make with it?
- Would people hold meetings about this? If so, the meeting's purpose is the real goal.
- If this task were automated away forever, what outcome would you want to stay true? ("Crash-free", not "fix this crash".)

## The escalation ladder

The essay's worked example is an imagined company's quarterly business review. Each rung is more ambitious than the last.

1. **Inputs.** Don't just refresh the numbers in the template. Give the model as much of the business as possible and ask what changed this quarter, why, and what to do about it.
2. **Decisions.** Meetings should end in decisions. Ask for the three most urgent decisions given everything learned, with possible directions and the arguments for and against each.
3. **Replace the artifact.** The review exists so leadership catches problems early and moves money and people. Ask for a better mechanism than a quarterly deck. Show from the company's own history that it would have caught problems sooner, then run it alongside the current process for a quarter.

Climb only as high as the user will act on. Propose the next rung and say what changes. Don't jump silently. *(ours)*

The third rung is always a proposal. Deliver the artifact that was asked for, at full craft, and offer the replacement alongside it. A landing page that has become an ordering app is a silent goal change, even when the app is good. *(ours)*

## Access is part of altitude

A higher-level goal usually needs infrastructure first. The essay's "keep the apps crash-free" goal only worked once the model could:

- fetch crash reports easily;
- map every app version to a git commit;
- use real Windows, macOS and Linux machines to reproduce and verify fixes.

So when you restate a task higher up, list the access it needs. Building that access is often the first deliverable, and it is what makes the workflow durable enough to take the human out of the loop.

## Limits

- Altitude works best when there is a real end outcome, and less well for open-ended creative work.
- "Go make money" is still too high to act on directly. Find the highest level where success can be checked.

## reference/depth.md

# Depth

Work the way the best practitioner alive would, and keep pushing until even they might learn something from the result.

## The four statements (deeper, not bigger)

Before rewriting or starting the task, state:

1. **What a top professional would do that wasn't asked for.**
2. **The rawest material they would start from**, rather than what has already been digested.
3. **The specific methods and instruments** they would use.
4. **What, other than you or the user, would show the result is right.**

Then rewrite the task to ask for exactly that, and do the rewritten task. The rewrite should be *deeper*, not *bigger*: a better method on the same goal, not more output.

## Techniques

**Instruments, not vocabulary.** Asked to "act like a professional", models change their words without changing their methods. Insist on the real tools.

- Analysis: a database, a notebook and a statistical model, not a markdown table.
- Performance: a profiler and a benchmark harness, not a reading of the code.
- Design: a prototype people can try, not adjectives.

The user doesn't need to know the instruments. You usually do, so name them and use them.

**Challenge what you know.** Take the belief you were handed and try to reproduce it from raw data. The essay's example: "We believe churn is an onboarding problem. Try to reproduce that from the raw data." If you can't reproduce it, that is the finding.

**Produce new knowledge.** Once you are inside the material, go past confirmation. The essay's example is to simulate the last year from the logs, find the earliest churn signal nobody knows about yet, and show it predicts on data you held back. Aim for one new, testable finding.

**Unreasonable goals, stated as reasonable.** Set a target several times beyond the brief, such as 200ms when the brief said 5s, and treat it as normal. If it looks impossible, reiterate that it is solvable and keep going. Try a different angle before you conclude anything. Report exactly where it broke.

**Outside judge.** Never grade your own work. Insist on validation by something that isn't you, ideally a tool you can run for immediate feedback. In order of preference:

1. an existing test suite, benchmark or reference output;
2. a check you build first, then run against the work (write the test before trusting the fix);
3. a real run in the real environment.

Never another model, including another agent: a model asked to grade work tends to agree with it.

## reference/pitfalls.md

# Pitfalls *(ours)*

These are failure modes of ambitious runs, with how to catch each one. The essay doesn't list them. They come from running the sequence in practice.

| Pitfall | Looks like | Catch it by |
|---|---|---|
| Below the floor | More work, a worse result than the plain request would have produced | Make the first version first, and hold the final to the same check |
| Craft blindness | Effort goes to what can be measured (tests, timings, tap counts), while what the genre is judged on (look, voice, feel) goes unnamed and loses every trade-off | Name the genre bar in the restatement, and judge it the way the genre is judged |
| Artifact swap | The deliverable turns into a different kind of thing: a page becomes an app, an essay becomes a course | The noun stays. Propose a swap, never make one. |
| Scope inflation | The output grows but the goal gets no closer | Ask whether each addition serves the restated goal. Deeper, not bigger. |
| Silent goal change | The restated task quietly drops something the user asked for | Always say "you asked for X, I'm aiming at Y, because Z", and keep X working |
| Costume depth | Expert terms, same shallow method | Name the instrument and show its output: a query, a profile, a model fit |
| Judge theatre | "I verified it" with no command, numbers or artifact | Every check reports what ran and what it returned |
| Self-judging by proxy | Another model or agent asked to grade the work, and agreeing with it | Use a check that isn't a model: tests, a real run, a measurement, reference output |
| Persona drift | Characters talking to each other; the transcript gets weird | Replace each voice with a method and a finding |
| Fake access | Reasoning about data you could have queried, or a machine you could have used | Stop and get the access, or ask for it |
| Ambition on trivia | A seven-step run on a one-line fix | Do a light pass. Proportion is part of judgment. |
| Stretch as excuse | Missing the actual brief while chasing the stretch | Meet the brief first and keep it passing, then stretch |
| Unrepeatable win | A great result that lives only in a transcript | The lock step: a script or spec, a CLAUDE.md note, a command |

## reference/range.md

# Range

Look at the work through several fields. That used to be too expensive to do routinely. Multi-agent setups make it cheap, and it is often where the most surprising results come from.

## Nouns to verbs

This technique comes from Tom Kelley and Jonathan Littman's *The Art of Innovation*. A noun locks you into one field. A verb shows you who else does the same thing.

- "A quarterly review deck" becomes "getting busy people to believe a story about cause and effect, and to decide under uncertainty, in 30 minutes".
- "A backup script" becomes "making sure a person can get their life's notes back after the worst day, without thinking".
- "An onboarding flow" becomes "getting a stranger to their first success before they lose interest".

Write the verb form first. Then ask which fields are best at each verb.

Keep the genre's own verbs in the list *(ours)*. A landing page still has to make people want what it sells, an essay still has to be a pleasure to read, and an API still has to feel obvious to its caller. Verbs find methods. They don't change what the deliverable is.

## Assemble the crew

Pick 3–5 fields that do those verbs differently, plus at least one whose job is to break the result. Always include the genre's own best practitioner *(ours)*: an art director for a page, an editor for prose, a seasoned maintainer for code. Without them, the crew optimises everything except the thing itself. The essay's crew for the review deck:

- **Production quality:** an analyst, a journalist and an editor.
- **If it will be presented:** a motion designer and an audio designer.
- **Red team:** a short seller and a forensic accountant.

The essay sets the stakes playfully ("the deck needs to be amazing, otherwise aliens will blow up Earth"). High, specific stakes beat "do your best".

## Do what they do, not how they sound

Role-play makes a transcript stranger without making the result better. Use personas only to find fields and methods.

- Wrong: "Write this like a short seller would."
- Right: "Do the research a short seller does before taking a position against this, and report what it finds."

For each field, name the concrete method you are borrowing: a checklist, a test, a format, a statistic, a review ritual. Then apply it.

## Using subagents

Give each field its own subagent when the work is big enough. Brief each with the verb form, the raw material and the specific method it should apply, and ask for findings rather than prose: a short list of what was found, with evidence, plus paths to any longer material. The red team should get the finished output and the goal, never your reasoning.

---

# Pushing on

The user chose to push the work further, one step at a time, the way a person runs one `/ambition` command after another in a single chat. Each step's instruction arrives on its own once the step before it is finished.

The work as it stands is the **first version**: it's in `.ambition/first/` (if it isn't, copy the deliverable there now, and add `.ambition/` to the project's .gitignore if it has one that doesn't cover it). You do the work yourself, in this conversation. Don't hand it to subagents; the only place they're welcome is Range, if several fields are worth exploring at once.

**Who answers.** By default, the user. Answer questions yourself only if the user told you to use your judgement (now or when pushing on); then answer from the repo, the conversation and sensible defaults, and list each answer as a labelled assumption.

**Plan or build.** If the user said plan or build, or plan mode is on, that decides it. Words like "plan", "design", "approach", "strategy", "proposal" or "options" mean plan; imperatives like "build", "fix", "add", "make", "ship", or an approved plan to carry out, mean build. When the deliverable is itself a document, improving it is the build. If it's unclear, make it your first question.
